Sinonasal cancer is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed progress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to evaluate a new radiation treatment known as Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT). A current method of radiation therapy used to treat canine sinonasal carcinoma (SC), called stereotactic body radiotherapy therapy (SBRT), distributes a high dose of radiation uniformly across the tumor. Lattice radiation therapy (LRT) differs from SBRT in that instead of administering that uniform high dose of radiation throughout the tumor, several small spheres of high dose radiation are administered within the tumor and the rest of the tumor receives a lower dose of radiation. LRT has shown promise in early studies to provide tumor control with low normal tissue toxicity, suspected to be due to improved blood flow and immune responses compared to uniform, high dose radiation therapy. Our goal is to look at the differences in the tumors immune response during and after treatment as well as the clinical response with LRT compared to our standard SBRT. Dogs enrolled into this study will be treated with LRT. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush under anesthesia. The following procedures will be performed in all dogs enrolled in the study: CT scan for radiation therapy planning Lattice radiation therapy; 3 treatments given once daily over consecutive business days under general anesthesia Nasal flush, 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Blood collection (9-19 mL), 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Tumor biopsy at the 2 week post-LRT time point under general anesthesia Recheck CT scan 3, 6, 12 months, and 18-months post-LRT under general anesthesia.
